findings.claim: Room E was initially cooling normally, then its door opened at 2026-03-26 00:48 UTC. The recovered controller record shows warming, repeated trips and lockout at 01:45, not an initiating permanent compressor failure.

A held-open door caused excess heat ingress and repeated protection trips; the fifth trip triggered a timed lockout, amplifying the excursion. Cooling subsequently resumed. This is the best-supported physical causal chain.

The postmortem identifies compressor failure on TK05 as the root cause. A permanent loss of cooling capacity is contradicted by pre-event cycling, protection events and sustained subsequent cooling; the compressor recall does not apply to the site NK-380 units.

Who opened or held room E open at 00:48 on March 26 cannot be determined. The controller proves the door state, not a person, and the evidence does not establish that Noor Costa caused this particular excursion.
alternatives: Noor Costa opened/held it while restocking.
Elif Dubois or another worker opened/held it.
The opener and the person who left it open were different. ROOM-E badge records and incident-week CCTV are missing.

findings.claim: Noor Costa probably used a wedge at room E earlier, by the March 16 00:40 photograph; the receipt, caption and contemporaneous chat contradict her blanket denial of ever propping a cold-room door, but do not identify the March 26 opener.

TK05 telemetry disappeared after the 00:48 door opening and resumed at 04:08 with a queue-overflow count of 53. The reproduced door-frame conduit/link fault in T-0410 is the best-supported explanation for the door-associated communications loss.

Room E reached at least +5.19 C controller air temperature at 04:10 March 26 (about +5.6 C after baseline bias correction). It then cooled, with a defrost at 07:42–08:08 delaying recovery; the incorrectly decoded reading cleared the old low-temperature alert at 04:10 instead of generating a high-temperature alarm.

The exact overnight room E peak, complete temperature path and every door/heater action between 00:48 and 04:08 cannot be uniquely reconstructed from the partial lockout snapshot and resumed telemetry.
alternatives: A continuously open door plus the observed trip/lockout rule and later recovery can explain the overnight trajectory.
Different unrecorded closure/reopening or heat-input histories can fit surviving endpoints. P1 sums A and E, and cannot uniquely allocate missing per-room activity.

findings.claim: Zara Byrne updated both E/TK05 and B/TK02 to firmware 3.4 on March 15, at 14:41 and 15:33 UTC respectively. The report saying TK05 was inspected only is contradicted by its 0034 boot banner and subsequent absolute-temperature flag.

Firmware 3.4 reports absolute temperatures; the deployed decoder continues to add each negative room setpoint. This creates the approximately -40 C readings in B and E. They are parser-induced, not evidence of the alleged new-board sensor defect.

The TK-5 wire map differs from the obsolete TK-7 card and the bench report: 67 is a trip, not a second defrost opcode; EB and 11 are synchronized defrost and heater events. The decoder recognizes only status air temperature and run/idle and ignores the other state meanings.

Ivan Novak authored routing hotfix 1a83340 on March 16 at 12:19:13. It routes all B/E alerts, including critical alerts, to the legacy channel, without changing thresholds. Jonas Nguyen archived that channel on March 17 at 10:03, before the excursion.

A separate untracked ALERT_MIN_SEVERITY=critical override was active, suppressing warnings, but its author and exact deployment time are not established. The routing commit does not identify its author; attributing it to Sofia Nguyen is unsupported.
alternatives: Sofia Nguyen could have deployed it despite her denial.
Ivan Novak or another person with host access could have deployed it. No shell/deployment audit or attributable versioned change survives.

findings.claim: Stale-controller warnings did not provide an independent alert path: the gateway posts controller_stale events, whereas alerting polls only latest temperature rows and performs no age check. Last-known temperatures can therefore look normal indefinitely while a controller is silent.

Nightly billing holds the ledger writer lock for roughly 31–45 minutes from 01:00. Ledger inserts fail and gateway frames are not acknowledged; controllers do not resend lost frames. This is a recurring monitoring blind spot, separate from the door-associated link failure and disk-full gap.

Billing exports use 1440 as daily hours rather than 24, a 60-fold unit error. Commit a99c183 introduced that error and 37f6e9e corrects it in git, but surviving later exports still contain 1440; a fix commit is not proof that the running billing process was corrected.

Scanner moves were not applied to the ledger: prefix routing sends GET /lots/<id> to get_lots, producing no top-level zone, and apply_move raises KeyError before PUT. Dispatch nevertheless marks failed jobs done. The ledger has zero moves and all 62 lots retain their import timestamp and position.

The move pipeline also permits duplicate jobs and large delays: inline serialized WMS lookup precedes durable enqueue/response, the gateway retries without an idempotency key, and the queue contains identical payloads under distinct job IDs. Successful enqueue/done status is not successful inventory reconciliation.

LN-26450 (PL-8620) was physically delivered into E by Ingrid Schulz at 16:33 March 25 after an F-to-C-to-E transfer, and Ana Novak picked it from E at 08:20 March 26 and dropped it in F at 08:22. The ledger incorrectly leaves it in F and the postmortem quarantine omits the lab-flagged lot.

The reconstructed prolonged overnight E exposure cohort is LN-24754, LN-28604 and LN-26450, not the five ledger-based quarantine lots. LN-25885 entered E at 09:07 during the recovery tail and also requires assessment, but its shorter exposure must not be equated with the overnight cohort.

All five lots named in the postmortem were elsewhere before the overnight excursion: LN-24872 in A; LN-26219, LN-26259 and LN-29864 in D; LN-28595 in F. Ledger-only quarantine both missed physically exposed lots and selected stale locations.

Ana Novak physically moved PL-1904/LN-22738 from F to B on March 27, picking at 07:32 and dropping at 07:34. Independent FL-1 telematics corroborates her statement; the failed dispatch job explains the unchanged ledger. Her unrelated speeding warning is not evidence of a false move.

Ingrid Schulz submitted an F-to-D scan for PL-9519/LN-25934 at 19:14 March 27, but the physical move itself cannot be independently confirmed. FL-2 telematics was dead and incident-week CCTV is expired; an unsuccessful ledger update does not decide whether the forklift moved.
alternatives: The pallet physically moved from F to D as stated, while the database update failed.
The scan did not correspond to the completed claimed physical move, or identified the wrong pallet/location. Missing FL-2 or CCTV evidence would distinguish these.

findings.claim: Room D developed a separate gradual positive sensor drift of about 3.1 C relative to its baseline, then returned toward baseline after April 3 recalibration. HH-2 is independently 1.1 C warm and out of tolerance; correcting that offset reverses the misleading claim that the handheld increasingly reads warmer than the panel.

Absolute sensor biases in C and F are not independently established: neither calibrated probe round covers those rooms. Shared-panel electricity and controller-only temperatures do not supply an independent absolute temperature reference.
alternatives: It could have a constant offset while the true temperature differs correspondingly; calibrated in-room reference measurements are missing.

findings.claim: Defrost cycles last 26 minutes and do not overlap. Their timing is consistent with about eight accumulated compressor-running hours plus shared scheduling, not a six-hour wall-clock cycle in each room. A complete fixed arbitration priority order is not uniquely established.

The March 14 utility interruption lasted approximately 10:49–11:11; all controller counters reset and services subsequently recovered. It is not evidence of a continuing supply failure causing the March 26 excursion.

The lab finding is consistent with LN-26450 spending hours above -15 C in E, but the surviving records do not establish each product core-temperature history, potency loss in every co-exposed lot, or an exclusive causal attribution for the lab result.
alternatives: The reconstructed warehouse exposure accounts for the degradation.
Other storage/transport exposures or lot-specific stability factors contributed as well. Product loggers, chain-of-custody temperatures and additional stability testing are absent.

findings.claim: The March 26 12:05–15:17 disk-full gap is a service-log gap, not a total evidence blackout: 231 raw readings survive in the ledger, including E cycling near setpoint and a door-open event at 15:14. Sofia Nguyen's assertion that nothing was written down is too broad.

The fourth status word behaves as discharge pressure, but its absolute engineering unit and scale cannot be independently established. The old integration note refers to an absent compressor data sheet; no pressure-reference measurements survive.
alternatives: For example, a word of 1140 could represent 114 units at scale 10.
It could instead represent 11.4 units at scale 100 (or another proportional convention). State correlation identifies the quantity but not a unique engineering-unit divisor.

findings.claim: A complete fixed defrost stagger/priority order is not uniquely reconstructed from the surviving starts: readiness, shared-heater exclusion and missing observations also determine which room goes next.
alternatives: First-ready requests may be serialized by the shared defrost resource.
A fixed tie-breaking priority may also operate, but the exact request counters and arbitration configuration needed to identify its full order do not survive.
